paragraphs.heading: Two starting rules
paragraphs.text: Special relativity rests on just two assumptions, both about observers moving at a constant speed relative to one another. The first, the principle of relativity, says the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, meaning any frame of reference that is not accelerating. The second says light in a vacuum travels at the same speed for every observer, however the source or the observer is moving. A great many results follow from these two rules.

paragraphs.heading: On a train
paragraphs.text: The first rule means physics does not depend on things being truly at rest. Someone on a train sees events on board behave the same way whether the train moves or stands still. Galileo described this idea in 1632, imagining what one would observe on a moving ship. The second rule is stranger: people in a station measure the same speed for light from inside the station and for light from a passing train. Light sent from the station to a train also arrives at the same speed, however fast the train goes.

paragraphs.heading: Time is local
paragraphs.text: The theory changes how we think about time most of all. Instead of one time flowing equally across the universe, each object has its own flow of time, which you can track by counting a clock's ticks. Two events that a clock at rest records as simultaneous happen at different times according to moving clocks. At ordinary speeds this slowing is too small to observe, but near the speed of light it becomes large.

paragraphs.heading: A built-in speed limit
paragraphs.text: Together, the two rules change what relative speed means. It is no longer simply distance divided by time; the speed of light is built in as the highest speed possible. So if a moving watch says you covered ten times as much ground in the same time, people on the ground will not see you go ten times faster. Speeds close to light's are called relativistic speeds, and at them many effects only make sense once special relativity is taken into account.

paragraphs.heading: A new geometry
paragraphs.text: Underneath, special relativity swaps Euclidean geometry for Lorentzian geometry. In Euclidean geometry, distances come from the Pythagorean theorem and use only space coordinates. In Lorentzian geometry, distances become intervals that also include time, entered with a minus sign. Unlike a distance in space, an interval between two events comes out equal for every observer, whatever their relative speed. To convert coordinates between two frames in relative motion, the Lorentz transformation takes the place of the Galilean transformation used in Newton's mechanics.

paragraphs.heading: Mass, energy and more
paragraphs.text: Combined with other laws of physics, the two rules predict that mass and energy are equivalent, written E = mc², with c standing for light's speed in a vacuum. The theory also explains how electricity and magnetism are related, and it adds corrections to the Doppler effect. One trap is that news of distant objects can travel no faster than light, so anything we see has already happened. That makes pictures of relativistic effects easy to get wrong.

paragraphs.heading: How it came about
paragraphs.text: In 1864 James Clerk Maxwell put forward a theory of electromagnetism that did not obey Galilean relativity: it predicted a constant speed of light in a vacuum, whatever the motion of its emitter or receiver. Experiments then tried to measure light's speed as Earth moved through a proposed fixed aether, ending with the Michelson–Morley experiment of 1887, which only confirmed the constant speed. Fixes proposed by FitzGerald, Lorentz and Poincaré all pointed toward something like special relativity. In 1916 relativity was extended to include gravity, as general relativity.
